Fatigue or decrement indices can be calculated using similar formulas to other RSA protocols, adapted for 7 sprints. In some protocols, this format is referred to as a phosphate-decrement or phosphate-recovery RSA test aimed at stressing phosphocreatine recovery.

instructions: This repeated sprint test includes a change of direction like you'd see in a game. You'll sprint 15 metres, turn sharply on the line, and sprint 15 metres back to the start, for a total of 30 metres each repetition. After each shuttle you'll have about 20–30 seconds to recover, then we'll repeat. We'll do a set number of shuttles, and I'll let you know when each sprint starts. Give a strong maximal effort each time, but stop immediately if you feel any sharp pain, chest symptoms, or dizziness and tell me straight away.
equipment_needed: Flat surface with 15 and 30 m markings; cones or tape; timing gates or stopwatch; timer for rest intervals; optional GPS or LPS for external load metrics
contraindications: Because change-of-direction sprinting imposes higher joint loads, avoid this test in athletes with recent knee, ankle, hip, or groin injury, or where sharp cutting is contraindicated. Standard high-intensity exercise contraindications also apply. Terminate if the athlete demonstrates unsafe cutting mechanics, reports joint instability, or develops concerning cardiopulmonary symptoms.
references:
Pyne et al. – Relationships Between Repeated Sprint Testing, Speed, and Endurance: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18714221/

Turner & Stewart – Repeat Sprint Ability in Team Sports: https://journals.lww.com/nsca-scj/fulltext/2013/02000/repeat_sprint_ability.5.aspx
scoring_system: Performance assessment is similar to straight-line RSA but also reflects change-of-direction ability. Faster best shuttle time and smaller performance decrement across the set indicate better repeated sprint and change-of-direction capacity. Coaches often find shuttle RSA especially relevant for court and field sports involving frequent decelerations and turns.
description: Repeated maximal shuttle sprints with change of direction

instructions: We are going to perform a maximal graded exercise test to directly assess your maximal oxygen uptake, or VO2max. This is a high-intensity test that will take you close to your physical limit. You will exercise on a treadmill or cycle while the workload increases step by step. We will monitor your heart rhythm, heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen use, and how you feel throughout. It is very important that you tell us immediately if you experience chest pain or pressure, unusual or severe shortness of breath, dizziness, feeling faint, palpitations, or any symptom that feels unsafe. You can stop the test at any time simply by telling us. Our team is here to keep you safe and we have emergency equipment available if needed.
equipment_needed: Motorised treadmill and/or cycle ergometer; calibrated metabolic cart for gas exchange; 12-lead ECG system or reliable heart rate monitoring; blood pressure equipment; RPE scale; emergency resuscitation equipment including defibrillator; trained clinicians experienced in advanced life support and exercise testing
contraindications: ABSOLUTE: acute MI (within 2 days), unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmias with hemodynamic compromise, symptomatic severe aortic stenosis, uncontrolled heart failure, acute PE/pulmonary infarction, acute myocarditis/pericarditis, acute aortic dissection, severe symptomatic hypertension. RELATIVE: significant stenotic valvular disease, moderate-severe hypertension, tachyarrhythmias/bradyarrhythmias, high-degree AV block. TERMINATE if: moderate-severe angina, marked dyspnoea, dizziness, near-syncope, poor perfusion, serious arrhythmias, ST elevation/significant depression, drop in SBP ≥10mmHg despite increasing workload, excessive BP rise, or client request.
references:
Beltz et al. – Graded Exercise Testing Protocols for Determination of VO2max: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5221270/

ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription: https://acsm.org/education-resources/books/guidelines-exercise-testing-prescription/

ACC/AHA Guideline Update for Exercise Testing: https://www.telecardiologo.com/descargas/21906.pdf

Fletcher et al. – Exercise Standards for Testing and Training: https://fd.org.ua/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Exercise-Standards-for-Testing-and-Training.pdf
scoring_system: VO2max testing is used to determine maximal aerobic capacity and to identify abnormal cardiopulmonary responses. A valid VO2max is typically indicated by: (1) plateau in VO2 despite increased workload; (2) RER ≥ 1.10; (3) HR near age-predicted max; (4) high RPE. VO2max values vary by age, sex, training status. Norms available in ACSM guidelines categorising from very low to high. VO2max is a powerful predictor of mortality and cardiovascular risk.
description: Gold standard maximal aerobic capacity assessment with gas analysis
search_tags: VO2max Testing – Maximal Graded Exercise Test (GXT)
name: VO2max Testing – Maximal Graded Exercise Test (GXT)

instructions: At the end of your exercise test, I'll ask you to slow down and recover either standing or sitting, depending on what is safest for you. I'll record your heart rate right at the end of the exercise and again at 1 minute and 2 minutes into recovery. The speed at which your heart rate falls helps us understand how your heart and nervous system respond to exercise. Please let me know if you feel lightheaded, dizzy, have chest discomfort, or feel unwell at any point during recovery so we can support you immediately.
equipment_needed: Reliable heart rate measurement (ECG, heart rate monitor, or validated telemetry); timer or stopwatch; safe recovery area (treadmill handrails, chair, or bed nearby)
contraindications: If heart rate fails to decrease appropriately or continues to rise in early recovery, or if the client develops angina, marked dyspnoea, hypotension, arrhythmias, or syncope, treat as potentially serious event and follow local emergency procedures. HRR measurement should occur in a setting prepared for adverse events, especially after maximal or high-risk exercise test.
references:
Cole et al. – Heart-Rate Recovery Immediately after Exercise as a Predictor of Mortality: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJM199910283411804

Cahalin & Arena – Heart Rate Recovery and Its Applications: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7293134/

Shetler et al. – Heart Rate Recovery: Validation and Methodologic Issues: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0735109701016527
scoring_system: Heart Rate Recovery is the fall in heart rate from peak exercise to a specified time point. Higher HRR (larger drop) indicates better autonomic function and cardiorespiratory fitness. HRR1 ≤ 12 bpm is associated with increased mortality risk, whereas larger declines (>15–20 bpm) are favourable. HRR2 values also predict outcomes. Interpretation considers recovery mode (active vs passive), beta-blocker use, and test protocol.
description: Post-exercise heart rate recovery measurement - prognostic marker
name: Heart Rate Recovery (HRR) – 1 and 2 Minutes

scoring.formula: HRR at each time point equals peak exercise heart rate minus heart rate at that recovery time point.

instructions: 1. Verify the patient’s identity using two forms of identification. 2. Confirm receipt of the latest HbA1c results from the laboratory and ensure they are part of the patient’s medical record. 3. Review the patient’s medical history and current medications, documenting any relevant changes or updates. 4. Analyze the HbA1c result according to the scoring system to classify the patient’s glycemic control status. 5. Discuss with the patient the implications of their HbA1c result, including potential health risks and recommended lifestyle modifications. 6. Inquire about relevant symptoms such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or fatigue and document them in the patient’s record as part of the assessment. 7. Compare the patient's results to established HbA1c target goals based on their individual health conditions (e.g., presence of diabetes, cardiovascular disease). 8. Educate the patient on the significance of maintaining glycemic control and provide resources for diet, exercise, and medication adherence. 9. If necessary, initiate a referral to an appropriate healthcare provider for further evaluation or management.
equipment_needed: 1. Current laboratory pathology report confirming HbA1c results. 2. Access to comprehensive patient medical history. 3. List of any current medications the patient is taking. 4. Standardized pre-exercise screening tools (e.g., PAR-Q) to assess readiness for physical activity. 5. Clinical symptom evaluation tools specific to diabetes (e.g., symptom questionnaire). 6. Interactive test runner for assessing immediate HbA1c needs and suggested interventions based on results.
contraindications: 1. Exercise professionals (EPs) must not perform blood sampling; HbA1c results must be derived from laboratory tests ordered by licensed healthcare practitioners. 2. Patients with HbA1c levels over 9% should undergo a comprehensive medical evaluation prior to engaging in exercise programs. 3. Immediate medical attention is warranted for symptoms like severe polyuria, polydipsia, unintended weight loss, or recurrent infections, indicative of acute diabetes complications.
references:
American Diabetes Association. (2020). 2. Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes—2020. Diabetes Care, 43(Suppl 1), S14-S31. https://doi.org/10.2337/dc20-S002 
International Diabetes Federation. (2019). IDF Diabetes Atlas, 9th edition. International Diabetes Federation. https://doi.org/10.48324/idf.2023.01
scoring_system: 1. HbA1c <5.7% (<39 mmol/mol): Normal range, indicates good glycemic control. 2. HbA1c 5.7–6.4% (39–46 mmol/mol): Indicates increased risk of diabetes or prediabetes, suggestive of lifestyle intervention. 3. HbA1c ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol): Diagnostic for diabetes, necessitating confirmatory testing and potential referral for management. Scores will result in tailored intervention plans based on disease risk and individual patient circumstances.
description: Interpretation of laboratory HbA1c results to assess average blood glucose control over 2-3 months
name: HbA1c (Glycated Hemoglobin)

scoring.formula: Direct HbA1c percentage classified by the existing threshold bands.
scoring.validation: Required values, units, enumerations, ranges, paired observations and finite derived results are enforced before persistence.

instructions: We're going to review your cholesterol and lipid results. These numbers help us understand your cardiovascular risk and how exercise and lifestyle can help. I'll look at your LDL (the 'bad' cholesterol), HDL (the 'good' cholesterol), triglycerides, and total cholesterol and then classify whether they're in healthy, borderline, or high-risk ranges. Please let me know if you're taking any cholesterol or triglyceride-lowering medications or if you have a personal or family history of heart disease or stroke.
equipment_needed: Recent laboratory lipid panel; cardiovascular and family history; medication list.
contraindications: EPs cannot order or perform lipid testing unless specifically credentialed and authorised. Interpretation only. Very high LDL-C (e.g., >5.0 mmol/L), very high triglycerides (e.g., >5.6 mmol/L), or lipid results associated with familial hypercholesterolaemia patterns should prompt strong recommendation for medical review. Chest pain, exertional dyspnoea, or other cardiac symptoms reported during exercise sessions require immediate cessation of exercise and appropriate escalation.
references:
National Vascular Disease Prevention Alliance / Heart Foundation – Lipid Management Guidelines: https://heartfoundation.org.au
ESC/EAS Guidelines for the Management of Dyslipidaemias: https://www.escardio.org/Guidelines
scoring_system:
Interpretation is risk-based rather than pass/fail. In general, lower LDL-C and non-HDL-C and higher HDL-C are associated with reduced risk. Common cut-points in many guidelines include approximately: LDL-C <2.0–2.6 mmol/L desirable (depending on risk category), 2.6–4.0 mmol/L borderline to high, and >4.0 mmol/L high. Triglycerides <1.7 mmol/L are considered desirable; 1.7–2.2 mmol/L borderline; >2.2 mmol/L high. HDL-C <1.0 mmol/L in men and <1.2 mmol/L in women is associated with increased risk.

Population norms vary by age, sex, and region. Most guidelines use target-based thresholds according to overall cardiovascular risk (e.g., primary vs secondary prevention) rather than strict age-based norms. Non-HDL-C and ApoB are sometimes used as additional markers where available.
description: Interpretation of laboratory lipid panel results to assess cardiovascular risk
name: Lipid Profile

scoring.formula: Direct total cholesterol result with LDL, HDL, triglycerides, unit, conversions and category bands retained.
scoring.validation: All required values, enumerations, nested observations, finite ranges and protocol constraints are enforced before persistence.

instructions: We're going to convert your exercise performance into METs. METs tell us how much energy you use during an activity compared to resting, and they help us classify exercise intensity and your overall fitness. We'll take your treadmill or bike workload and use standard equations to estimate your VO2 and then convert that into METs. This helps us prescribe exercise that's safe but still challenging.
equipment_needed: Data from a graded exercise test or field test (e.g., treadmill speed/grade, cycle wattage); ACSM metabolic equations or equivalent reference; calculator or software for VO2 and METs.
contraindications: If the estimated MET capacity is markedly lower than expected for the client's age and health status, especially if accompanied by chest pain, abnormal blood pressure response, significant desaturation, or severe dyspnoea during the test, medical review is recommended. Estimation should not be used in place of formal clinical exercise testing when indicated.
references:
ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription – Metabolic Calculations: https://acsm.org/education-resources/books/guidelines-exercise-testing-prescription/
Ainsworth BE et al. – Compendium of Physical Activities (MET Values): https://prevention.sph.sc.edu/tools/compendium.htm
scoring_system:
Higher MET capacity generally indicates better aerobic fitness and more favourable health prognosis. As a rough guide, peak capacity <5 METs is low, 5–10 METs is moderate, and >10 METs is high for many adults, though exact cut-offs vary by age and guideline. MET thresholds are also used to classify individual activities (light <3 METs, moderate 3–6 METs, vigorous >6 METs).

Normative MET capacities and VO2max values are available in ACSM and other exercise-testing and rehabilitation references and are usually stratified by age and sex. These tables can be loaded into Base44 as separate look-up references rather than embedded as fixed cut-offs.
description: Calculation of metabolic equivalents from exercise test data to classify aerobic capacity
name: Metabolic Equivalent (MET) Calculation

instructions: This test measures how your heart and lungs cope with continuous stepping. You'll step up and down on this step at a comfortable pace you feel you can maintain for six minutes. You can hold the rail if needed for balance. If at any time you feel chest pain, severe shortness of breath, dizziness, or anything that feels unsafe, please tell me immediately and we'll stop the test. You can stop at any time if you need to rest.
equipment_needed: Sturdy step of known and documented height; stopwatch or timer; optional handrail; heart rate monitor; sphygmomanometer or automated BP monitor; pulse oximeter; RPE scale.
contraindications: Do not perform the test in individuals with unstable angina, uncontrolled arrhythmias, recent myocardial infarction or surgery, uncontrolled severe hypertension, acute respiratory distress, resting SpO2 below protocol-specific safety thresholds (e.g., <88–90%), or where balance impairment makes stepping unsafe. Terminate the test if the client reports chest pain, intolerable dyspnoea, dizziness, near-syncope, severe leg pain, or if SpO2 or blood pressure move outside safe parameters.
references:
Mendes et al. – Six-Minute Step Test in Healthy Adults and Patients with Chronic Disease: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
Rehabilitation Measures Database – 6-Minute Step Test: https://www.sralab.org/rehabilitation-measures/6-minute-step-test
scoring_system:
This is a functional capacity test rather than a pass/fail test. A higher total step count generally indicates better submaximal functional capacity. Clinicians may compare step count and physiological responses (HR, SpO2, symptoms) with normative data or previous tests to evaluate capacity and change over time. Abnormal responses include marked desaturation (e.g., SpO2 falling below clinically acceptable thresholds), excessive tachycardia, severe dyspnoea, chest pain, or other concerning symptoms.

Normative values for the 6-Minute Step Test vary based on step height, protocol, age, and clinical population. Published studies provide reference ranges for older adults, people with cardiac or pulmonary disease, and healthy individuals. Because protocols differ, clinicians should specify step height and reference which normative dataset is being used rather than applying a single normative table.
description: Functional aerobic capacity test measuring number of steps completed in 6 minutes
name: 6-Minute Step Test

instructions: We're going to complete a series of short tasks that reflect everyday activities, such as standing up from a chair, putting on a jacket, picking up a small object from the floor, and walking. I'll time or score each task based on how you perform it. Please do each task to the best of your ability, but stop and tell me if you feel unsafe, very unsteady, or have any unusual pain or symptoms.
equipment_needed: Chair with arms; stopwatch; lightweight jacket or coat; small object such as a coin; writing instrument and paper; hallway or safe walking space for gait items.
contraindications: Avoid or modify tasks in individuals with severe balance impairment, high falls risk, or acute musculoskeletal injury that could be exacerbated by the tasks (e.g., severe back pain, unstable fracture). Stop testing immediately if the client becomes dizzy, experiences chest pain, or appears at risk of falling. Consider having a gait belt and close supervision for clients with significant mobility limitations.
references:
Reuben & Siu – An Objective Measure of Physical Function of Elderly Outpatients: The Physical Performance Test: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2109756/
Rehabilitation Measures Database – Physical Performance Test (PPT): https://www.sralab.org/rehabilitation-measures/physical-performance-test
scoring_system:
Higher PPT total scores indicate better functional performance in activities of daily living. Lower scores suggest declining function, frailty, or increased risk of loss of independence. In the original PPT, total scores below certain thresholds (e.g., around 19 for the 9-item version) have been associated with increased risk of disability and institutionalisation, although exact cut-points depend on the version and population.

Normative and cut-point data are available for older adults living in the community and in institutional settings. These data relate PPT scores to functional status, frailty, and risk of adverse events. Because different PPT versions (7-item, 9-item) exist, Base44 should allow the assessor to specify which version is used and interpret scores accordingly.
description: Standardized battery of functional tasks to assess physical performance in older adults
name: Physical Performance Test (PPT)

instructions:
**Step-by-Step Protocol for Administering the PHQ-9:**

1. **Preparation:**
   - Ensure a private and comfortable setting to maintain patient confidentiality.
   - Provide the patient with a copy of the PHQ-9 questionnaire.

2. **Introduction:**
   - Explain the purpose of the PHQ-9: "This questionnaire is designed to help us understand how you've been feeling over the past two weeks. Your responses will assist in assessing your mood and identifying any symptoms of depression."
   - Emphasize that there are no right or wrong answers and that honesty is crucial for accurate assessment.

3. **Administration:**
   - Instruct the patient to read each statement carefully and indicate how often they have been bothered by each problem during the past two weeks.
   - Responses are scored as follows:
     - 0 = Not at all
     - 1 = Several days
     - 2 = More than half the days
     - 3 = Nearly every day
   - Ensure the patient understands the scoring system.

4. **Completion:**
   - After the patient completes the questionnaire, review their responses to ensure clarity and completeness.
   - If any items are left unanswered, ask the patient to provide responses.

5. **Scoring:**
   - Sum the scores of all nine items to obtain a total score ranging from 0 to 27.

6. **Interpretation:**
   - Refer to the scoring system to interpret the total score:
     - 0–4: Minimal or no depression
     - 5–9: Mild depression
     - 10–14: Moderate depression
     - 15–19: Moderately severe depression
     - 20–27: Severe depression
   - Discuss the results with the patient, providing appropriate feedback and recommendations based on the score.

7. **Follow-Up:**
   - If the total score is 10 or higher, consider referring the patient for further psychological or psychiatric assessment to evaluate for possible depressive disorder.
   - For scores below 10, monitor the patient's symptoms over time and provide support as needed.

**Contraindications (Safety Considerations):**

- **Suicidal Ideation:**
  - If the patient endorses thoughts of self-harm or suicide (i.e., scores 1 or higher on item 9), immediate and direct follow-up is required.
  - Conduct a thorough suicide risk assessment and develop a safety plan, which may include involving family members or referring the patient for emergency psychiatric evaluation.

- **Cognitive Impairment:**
  - Patients with significant cognitive impairments may have difficulty understanding or accurately completing the questionnaire.
  - In such cases, consider alternative assessment methods or involve a caregiver to assist in the process.

**Equipment Needed:**

- **Paper-Based Questionnaire:**
  - A printed copy of the PHQ-9 form for the patient to complete.

- **Writing Instrument:**
  - A pen or pencil for the patient to mark their responses.

- **Scoring Sheet:**
  - A separate sheet or form to record and calculate the total score.

**Scoring System:**

- **Individual Item Scoring:**
  - Each of the nine items is rated on a 4-point scale:
    - 0 = Not at all
    - 1 = Several days
    - 2 = More than half the days
    - 3 = Nearly every day

- **Total Score Calculation:**
  - Sum the scores of all nine items to obtain a total score ranging from 0 to 27.

- **Interpretation of Total Score:**
  - 0–4: Minimal or no depression
  - 5–9: Mild depression
  - 10–14: Moderate depression
  - 15–19: Moderately severe depression
  - 20–27: Severe depression

- **Treatment Recommendations Based on Total Score:**
  - 0–4: None – minimal
  - 5–9: Minimal symptoms – Support, educate to call if worse, return in one month
  - 10–14: Minor depression – Support, watchful waiting
  - 15–19: Major depression, moderately severe – Antidepressant and/or psychotherapy
  - 20–27: Major depression, severe – Antidepressant AND psychotherapy (especially if not improved on monotherapy)

*Note: The PHQ-9 is a screening tool and should not replace a comprehensive clinical evaluation.*

instructions:
1. **Administering the GAD-7**:
   - **Self-Administration**: Provide the patient with the GAD-7 questionnaire and instruct them to read each statement carefully.
   - **Response Options**: For each item, the patient selects one of the following responses based on their experience over the past two weeks:
     - 0: Not at all
     - 1: Several days
     - 2: More than half the days
     - 3: Nearly every day
   - **Completion Time**: The questionnaire typically takes 2-5 minutes to complete. ([rbhi.org](https://www.rbhi.org/gad7?utm_source=openai))
   - **Assistance**: If the patient has difficulty reading or understanding the questions, an interviewer can read the items aloud and record the patient's responses.

2. **Scoring the GAD-7**:
   - **Assign Scores**: Each response is scored as follows:
     - 0: Not at all
     - 1: Several days
     - 2: More than half the days
     - 3: Nearly every day
   - **Calculate Total Score**: Sum the scores of all seven items to obtain a total score ranging from 0 to 21.

3. **Interpreting the Results**:
   - **Severity Levels**:
     - 0-4: Minimal Anxiety
     - 5-9: Mild Anxiety
     - 10-14: Moderate Anxiety
     - 15-21: Severe Anxiety
   - **Clinical Significance**: A total score of 10 or higher suggests a clinically significant level of anxiety and warrants further evaluation. ([rbhi.org](https://www.rbhi.org/gad7?utm_source=openai))

4. **Follow-Up**:
   - If the patient's score indicates moderate to severe anxiety, consider referring them to a mental health professional for a comprehensive assessment and potential treatment.
   - For patients with mild anxiety, monitor their symptoms over time and provide appropriate support or interventions as needed.

**Contraindications**:
- **Cognitive Impairment**: Patients with significant cognitive impairments may have difficulty understanding or accurately completing the questionnaire, potentially leading to unreliable results.
- **Severe Distress**: If a patient is in acute distress or experiencing a crisis, administering the GAD-7 may not be appropriate until their immediate needs are addressed.
- **Language Barriers**: Ensure that the patient can understand the language in which the questionnaire is presented. If not, consider providing a translated version or using an interpreter.

**Equipment Needed**:
- **GAD-7 Questionnaire**: Available in various formats, including paper copies and digital versions.
- **Writing Instrument**: For patients completing the questionnaire manually.
- **Computer or Tablet**: If administering a digital version.
- **Interpreter Services**: If language assistance is required.

**Scoring System**:
- **Assign Scores**: Each response is scored as follows:
  - 0: Not at all
  - 1: Several days
  - 2: More than half the days
  - 3: Nearly every day
- **Calculate Total Score**: Sum the scores of all seven items to obtain a total score ranging from 0 to 21.
- **Interpretation**:
  - 0-4: Minimal Anxiety
  - 5-9: Mild Anxiety
  - 10-14: Moderate Anxiety
  - 15-21: Severe Anxiety
- **Clinical Significance**: A total score of 10 or higher suggests a clinically significant level of anxiety and warrants further evaluation. ([rbhi.org](https://www.rbhi.org/gad7?utm_source=openai))

*Note: The GAD-7 is a screening tool and should not be used as a sole basis for diagnosing generalized anxiety disorder. A comprehensive clinical assessment is necessary for a definitive diagnosis.*

instructions:
1. **Preparation**: Ensure the participant is comfortable and understands the purpose of the Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale, which measures the intensity of physical activity based on personal perception.

2. **Introduction to the Scale**: Explain that the scale ranges from 6 to 20, where 6 represents 'no exertion at all' and 20 signifies 'maximal exertion'. ([med.umich.edu](https://www.med.umich.edu/1libr/Stroke/BorgScale?utm_source=openai))

3. **During Activity**: While the participant engages in the physical activity, periodically ask them to rate their perceived exertion using the scale. Encourage honest self-assessment to accurately gauge exercise intensity.

4. **Post-Activity Assessment**: After completing the activity, request a final RPE rating to evaluate the overall intensity experienced.

5. **Documentation**: Record the RPE scores at each interval and the final score for analysis.

6. **Feedback**: Discuss the ratings with the participant to understand their perception of the activity's intensity and adjust future exercise plans accordingly.

**Note**: Familiarizing the participant with the scale before the activity can enhance the accuracy of their assessments.
equipment_needed: No specialized equipment is required to administer the Borg RPE scale. A printed or digital version of the scale for reference is recommended.
contraindications: The Borg RPE scale is a subjective measure and may not be suitable for individuals who have difficulty self-assessing their exertion levels due to cognitive impairments or language barriers. Additionally, it may not be appropriate for those with severe cardiovascular or respiratory conditions where precise monitoring of physiological parameters is essential.
references: Cleveland Clinic – Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion Scale: https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/17450-borg-rating-of-perceived-exertion-rpe-scale - The Borg RPE scale ranges from 6 (no exertion) to 20 (maximal exertion).
scoring_system:
The Borg RPE scale assigns numbers to perceived exertion levels:

- **6**: No exertion at all
- **7**: Extremely light
- **8**: 
- **9**: Very light
- **10**: 
- **11**: Light
- **12**: 
- **13**: Somewhat hard
- **14**: 
- **15**: Hard (heavy)
- **16**: 
- **17**: Very hard
- **18**: 
- **19**: Extremely hard
- **20**: Maximal exertion

These ratings correspond to the participant's subjective perception of exercise intensity, aiding in monitoring and adjusting exercise programs. ([med.umich.edu](https://www.med.umich.edu/1libr/Stroke/BorgScale?utm_source=openai))
description: The Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) scale allows individuals to subjectively rate the intensity of physical activity. The original scale ranges from 6 (no exertion) to 20 (maximal exertion). Moderate-intensity activity corresponds to ratings of 12–14. A modified CR10 scale runs from 0 (nothing at all) to 10 (very, very heavy). Participants consider factors such as breathing rate, heart rate, muscle fatigue and sweat when selecting a number.
name: Borg RPE (Rating of Perceived Exertion)

scoring.formula: Direct rating on the explicitly selected Borg 6–20 or modified CR10 scale.
scoring.validation: All required values, enumerations, nested observations, finite ranges and protocol constraints are enforced before persistence.

instructions:
SETUP:
1. Clear walkway (at least 3 meters)
2. Standard armchair
3. Stopwatch
4. Clear space for turning

CLINICIAN SCRIPT TO CLIENT:
"This test evaluates your balance and walking ability. I'll observe you performing different activities - some while sitting and standing, others while walking. I'll score each activity based on how well you perform it. I'll be close by to ensure your safety throughout the test."

PART I - BALANCE (9 items, 16 points):
1. SITTING BALANCE: "Sit in the chair" - Observe if steady
2. RISING FROM CHAIR: "Stand up" - Note use of arms, balance
3. IMMEDIATE STANDING BALANCE: Observe first 3-5 seconds standing
4. STANDING BALANCE: "Stand still" - Observe for 1 minute
5. BALANCE WITH EYES CLOSED: "Close your eyes and stand still"
6. TURNING 360°: "Turn in a complete circle, pause, then turn in the other direction"
7. SITTING DOWN: "Please sit down" - Observe control
8. NUDGE TEST: Gently nudge sternum 3 times while client stands with feet close together
9. STANDING ON ONE LEG: "Stand on one leg as long as you can"

PART II - GAIT (7 items, 12 points):
1. GAIT INITIATION: "Walk at your normal pace"
2. STEP LENGTH & HEIGHT: Observe right and left swing
3. STEP SYMMETRY: Compare right and left steps
4. STEP CONTINUITY: Observe flow of steps
5. PATH DEVIATION: Observe straight line walking
6. TRUNK STABILITY: Note sway or arm use for balance
7. WALKING STANCE: Observe heel-to-heel distance

SCORING:
- Balance section: 0-16 points
- Gait section: 0-12 points
- Total: 0-28 points
contraindications: Severe cognitive impairment, inability to stand independently, acute illness, severe pain limiting movement
references:
Tinetti ME. Performance-oriented assessment of mobility problems in elderly patients. J Am Geriatr Soc. 1986;34(2):119-126.

Tinetti ME, Williams TF, Mayewski R. Fall risk index for elderly patients based on number of chronic disabilities. Am J Med. 1986;80(3):429-434.

Raîche M, Hébert R, Prince F, Corriveau H. Screening older adults at risk of falling with the Tinetti balance scale. Lancet. 2000;356(9234):1001-1002.
scoring_system:
Total score 0-28 points (Balance 0-16 + Gait 0-12).

Interpretation:
• 25-28: Low fall risk
• 19-24: Medium fall risk (2x risk)
• <19: High fall risk (5x risk)

Balance subscale <13 or Gait subscale <10 indicates high risk.
description: Comprehensive assessment evaluating balance and gait performance to predict fall risk in older adults.
name: Tinetti Performance Oriented Mobility Assessment

name: 6-Minute Walk Test
description: Measures the distance an individual can walk in 6 minutes on a flat, hard surface to evaluate functional exercise capacity and endurance.
instructions:
SETUP:
1. Mark 30-meter straight course with cones at each end
2. Prepare chair for rest if needed
3. Set up pulse oximeter and blood pressure cuff
4. Position stopwatch

PRE-TEST:
1. Measure baseline vitals: HR, BP, SpO2, RPE
2. Check for contraindications
3. Ensure client comfortable with equipment

STANDARDIZED INSTRUCTIONS (READ TO CLIENT):
"You are now going to do a 6 minute walk test. The object of this test is to walk as far as you can for six minutes so that you cover as much ground as possible.

You may slow down if necessary. If you stop, I want you to continue to walk again as soon as possible.

You will be regularly informed of the time and you will be encouraged to do your best. Your goal is to walk as far as possible in six minutes, but don't run or jog.

Please do not talk during the test unless you have a problem or I ask you a question. You must let me know if you have any chest pain or dizziness.

When the six minutes is up I will ask you to stop where you are. Do you have any questions?"

DURING TEST:
- Start timer when saying "Start walking now."
- Give standardized encouragement each minute:
  • 1 min: "You are doing well. You have 5 minutes to go."
  • 2 min: "Keep up the good work. You have 4 minutes to go."
  • 3 min: "You are doing well. You are halfway."
  • 4 min: "Keep up the good work. You have only 2 minutes left."
  • 5 min: "You are doing well. You have only 1 minute to go."
  • 6 min: "Please stop where you are."
- Count laps completed
- Record any rest periods with times and reasons
- Monitor for signs of distress

POST-TEST:
1. Stop client at exactly 6 minutes
2. Immediately measure: HR, SpO2, RPE, dyspnea (0-10 scale)
3. Calculate total distance (30m × complete laps + partial distance)
4. Allow recovery while seated
5. Record observations and notes
scoring_system:
Distance walked in meters. Compare to age, gender, height, and weight predicted values using equations:

Men: 6MWD(m) = (7.57 × height cm) - (5.02 × age) - (1.76 × weight kg) - 309m
Women: 6MWD(m) = (2.11 × height cm) - (2.29 × weight kg) - (5.78 × age) + 667m

Interpretation:
• <350m: Severe impairment
• 350-450m: Moderate impairment
• >450m: Mild/normal for most populations
• Healthy adults: typically 400-700m

Clinically meaningful difference: 30-50m change
equipment_needed: 30-meter hallway or track, measuring wheel or tape, cones (2), stopwatch, chair for rest, pulse oximeter, blood pressure cuff, clipboard with data sheet, Borg RPE scale
contraindications:
ABSOLUTE:
- Unstable angina in previous month
- Myocardial infarction within previous month
- Resting heart rate >120 bpm
- Systolic BP >180 mmHg
- Diastolic BP >100 mmHg

RELATIVE:
- Known moderate stenotic heart valve disease
- Electrolyte abnormalities
- Severe arterial hypertension (>200/110)
- Tachyarrhythmias or bradyarrhythmias
- Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
- High-degree atrioventricular block

STOP TEST IF:
- Chest pain or angina
- Intolerable dyspnea
- Leg cramps
- Staggering, lightheadedness, confusion
- Diaphoresis
- Pale or ashen appearance
- SpO2 drops below 80%
references:
ATS Committee on Proficiency Standards for Clinical Pulmonary Function Laboratories. ATS statement: guidelines for the six-minute walk test. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2002;166(1):111-117.

Enright PL, Sherrill DL. Reference equations for the six-minute walk in healthy adults. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1998;158(5):1384-1387.

Casanova C, Celli BR, Barria P, et al. The 6-min walk distance in healthy subjects: reference standards from seven countries. Eur Respir J. 2011;37(1):150-156.

Polkey MI, Spruit MA, Edwards LD, et al. Six-minute-walk test in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: minimal clinically important difference for death or hospitalization. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2013;187(4):382-386.

scoring.formula: Device- or clinician-recorded total distance walked during the timed protocol.
scoring.validation: Every required value, nested field, choice, bound and protocol relationship is validated before persistence.

instructions: Select the joints to assess, then for each movement select the % ROM achieved (Full/¾/½/¼/Minimal/Unable) and whether the client reports pain. Add optional quick notes per movement. A summary and SOAP text is auto-generated on completion.
scoring_system: Each movement scored as % of normal ROM (0–100%) plus pain status (yes/no). Overall score = mean % ROM across all assessed movements.
description: A visual, clinician-guided range of motion screening tool. The clinician takes the client through all joint movements and records % ROM achieved and whether pain is reported — no goniometer required.
name: Visual ROM Assessment

scoring.formula: Arithmetic mean of every completed movement across selected joints; all selected movements must have ROM and pain recorded.
scoring.validation: Required fields, choice domains, trial cardinality and numeric bounds are enforced before scoring; invalid input throws and does not persist.

source_content.instructions:
SETUP:
1. Quiet, private environment
2. DASS-21 questionnaire form
3. Allow 5-10 minutes

CLINICIAN SCRIPT TO CLIENT:
"This questionnaire has 21 statements about your emotional experiences over the past week. It measures three areas: depression, anxiety, and stress. For each statement, you'll rate how much it applied to you over the past week using a scale from 0 to 3, where:
0 = Did not apply to me at all
1 = Applied to me to some degree, or some of the time
2 = Applied to me a considerable degree or a good part of the time
3 = Applied to me very much or most of the time

There are no right or wrong answers. Don't spend too much time on any statement - your first response is usually the most accurate. Please answer all questions honestly."

ADMINISTRATION:
1. Can be self-administered or clinician-read
2. Emphasize past 7 days timeframe
3. Clarify the 4-point rating scale
4. Ensure all 21 items completed
5. Check for consistency in responses

SCORING:
Calculate three subscales separately:
- Depression: Items 3,5,10,13,16,17,21 (multiply sum by 2)
- Anxiety: Items 2,4,7,9,15,19,20 (multiply sum by 2)
- Stress: Items 1,6,8,11,12,14,18 (multiply sum by 2)

INTERPRETATION:
DEPRESSION: 0-9 Normal, 10-13 Mild, 14-20 Moderate, 21-27 Severe, 28+ Extremely Severe
ANXIETY: 0-7 Normal, 8-9 Mild, 10-14 Moderate, 15-19 Severe, 20+ Extremely Severe
STRESS: 0-14 Normal, 15-18 Mild, 19-25 Moderate, 26-33 Severe, 34+ Extremely Severe

FEEDBACK:
"Your results show:
- Depression: [score] - [severity]
- Anxiety: [score] - [severity]
- Stress: [score] - [severity]

This helps us understand which areas are most challenging for you right now. [Discuss elevated subscales and implications]. How do these results align with how you've been feeling?"
source_content.equipment_needed: DASS-21 form, pen, calculator, private space
source_content.contraindications: Severe cognitive impairment, acute psychosis, language barriers without translation
source_content.references:
Lovibond SH, Lovibond PF. Manual for the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales. 2nd ed. Sydney: Psychology Foundation; 1995.

Henry JD, Crawford JR. The short-form version of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales (DASS-21): Construct validity and normative data in a large non-clinical sample. Br J Clin Psychol. 2005;44(Pt 2):227-239.
source_content.scoring_system: Three subscales: Depression (0-42), Anxiety (0-42), Stress (0-42). Higher scores indicate more severe symptoms.

name: Air Displacement Plethysmography (BOD POD)
description: Records BOD POD air-displacement plethysmography output for body volume, density, fat mass, fat-free mass and body-fat percentage.
instructions: Use the BOD POD manufacturer protocol. Before testing, fast for two hours, avoid exercise for eight hours, wear minimal tight-fitting clothing and remove jewellery. Record the device outputs; body-fat percentage can be entered directly or calculated when body mass and fat mass are both recorded.
scoring_system: Primary result is body-fat percentage. When it is not supplied directly, calculate fat mass divided by body mass multiplied by 100. Fat-free mass may be calculated as body mass minus fat mass. Preserve the remaining device outputs without applying an unreferenced universal classification.
equipment_needed: Calibrated BOD POD system, scale, swim cap and tight-fitting test clothing.
contraindications: Follow device-specific contraindications and manufacturer instructions; the patient must be able to sit safely in the sealed chamber for the measurement interval.
references: Dempster P, Aitkens S. A new air displacement method for the determination of human body composition. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 1995;27(12):1692–1697. Siri WE. The gross composition of the body. Advances in Biological and Medical Physics. 1956;4:239–280.

name: Balance Error Scoring System (BESS)
description: Six-condition static balance error assessment using double-leg, single-leg and tandem stances on firm and foam surfaces.
instructions: Hands remain on the iliac crests and eyes remain closed for each 20-second condition. Score one error for lifting hands, opening eyes, stepping/stumbling/falling, hip abduction beyond 30 degrees, lifting forefoot or heel, or remaining out of position for more than five seconds. Cap each condition at 10 errors; score 10 if the position cannot be maintained for at least five seconds.
scoring_system: Sum errors across all six completed conditions for a total from 0 to 60; lower scores represent better balance control. Interpret the total against the applicable individual baseline and population context rather than applying a universal severity band.
equipment_needed: Stopwatch, firm floor, foam balance surface and a spotter.
contraindications: Acute ankle or knee injury, severe dizziness or acute vestibular dysfunction are relative contraindications. Spot every condition and stop when the patient is at risk of falling.
references: Riemann BL, Guskiewicz KM, Shields EW. Relationship between clinical and forceplate measures of postural stability. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 1999;8(2):71–82. Guskiewicz KM et al. Postural stability and neuropsychological deficits after concussion. Journal of Athletic Training. 2001;36(3):263–273.

name: Edmonton Frail Scale (EFS)
description: Eleven scored items across cognition, general health, functional independence, social support, medication use, nutrition, mood, continence and functional performance.
instructions: Administer all eleven items. The clock task and Timed Up and Go are performance based. If the clock score is 1 or 2, an accompanying person may provide input for marked historical items; otherwise the interviewee answers the questions.
scoring_system: Sum all eleven item values for a total from 0 to 17; higher scores indicate greater frailty. The maintained interpretation bands are 0–4 not frail, 5–6 apparently vulnerable, 7–8 mildly frail, 9–10 moderately frail and 11–17 severely frail.
equipment_needed: Pre-drawn clock circle, pen, chair, three-metre walkway and stopwatch.
contraindications: Use appropriate support for the Timed Up and Go task and record inability, unwillingness or required assistance using the defined response option.

name: Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS)
description: Records a clinician-determined EDSS rating and optional functional-system grades for multiple-sclerosis disability.
instructions: Complete the neurological examination and determine the EDSS rating using the full scale criteria. Record the overall EDSS score from 0 to 10 and, when available, grades for pyramidal, cerebellar, brainstem, sensory, bowel and bladder, visual, cerebral and ambulation functional systems.
scoring_system: Record the clinician-determined EDSS value: 0 is a normal neurological examination; 1.0–3.5 reflects minimal to moderate disability while fully ambulatory; 4.0–5.5 reflects ambulatory disability without aid; 6.0–6.5 requires walking aid; 7.0–7.5 is wheelchair dependence; 8.0–9.5 is bed or chair restriction; 10 is death due to multiple sclerosis.
equipment_needed: Neurological examination equipment and the EDSS scoring criteria.
contraindications: This is a clinician-recorded scale. Determination of the score requires appropriate neurological assessment training.
references: Kurtzke JF. Rating neurologic impairment in multiple sclerosis: an expanded disability status scale (EDSS). Neurology. 1983;33(11):1444–1452.

name: International Physical Activity Questionnaire – Short Form (IPAQ-SF)
description: Seven-item last-seven-days recall of vigorous activity, moderate activity, walking and weekday sitting time.
instructions: Ask every item for the last seven days. Count vigorous activity, moderate activity and walking only when performed for at least 10 minutes at a time. Record days per week and the usual minutes per active day; record sitting time for a weekday.
scoring_system: Continuous score is MET-minutes per week: vigorous days × minutes × 8.0, moderate days × minutes × 4.0, and walking days × minutes × 3.3; total is the sum of those three domains. Categorisation uses the IPAQ short-form activity criteria and must use the same validated scoring implementation as the runner.
contraindications: Not applicable to questionnaire administration; interpretation depends on complete, plausible recall data.

name: Timed Up and Down Stairs (TUDS)
description: Performance measure of the time required to ascend, turn and descend a flight of stairs quickly and safely.
instructions: Position the patient 30 cm from the bottom of a 14-step flight. On the start cue, the patient goes up the stairs quickly but safely, turns on the top step or landing, and returns until both feet reach the bottom landing. Record elapsed seconds, stair configuration, rail or assistive-device use and safety observations.
scoring_system: Primary result is elapsed time in seconds; lower time represents faster functional stair mobility. Preserve every trial and report average and best time. Do not apply adult severity bands to the original paediatric protocol without population-specific evidence.
equipment_needed: Stopwatch and a 14-step flight of stairs with handrail access.
contraindications: Acute lower-limb injury, severe stair pain, marked unsupported balance impairment or recent surgery affecting mobility. Provide close supervision and stop for pain, distress or unsafe performance.
references: Zaino CA, Marchese VG, Westcott SL. Timed up and down stairs test: preliminary reliability and validity of a new measure of functional mobility. Pediatric Physical Therapy. 2004;16(2):90–98. doi:10.1097/01.PEP.0000127564.08922.6A.

name: Neurological Screening Examination
description: Structured screen of myotomes, dermatomes and deep tendon reflexes for the upper or lower limb.
instructions: Test each myotome against resistance, each dermatome for light touch and sharp or blunt discrimination, and the relevant deep tendon reflexes. Record findings by level and by side, and note any asymmetry.
scoring_system: Recorded per level and side as normal, reduced or absent. Reflexes graded 0 to 4 on the standard scale.
contraindications: None

rights.note: A standard clinical examination sequence rather than a proprietary instrument.

name: QuickDASH
description: Eleven-item measure of upper limb disability and symptoms. Score capture only in this build.
instructions: This platform does not reproduce the questionnaire. Administer the instrument from your own licensed copy and record the resulting score here.
scoring_system: Eleven items, transformed to a score from 0 (no disability) to 100 (most severe disability).
equipment_needed: Your own licensed copy of the instrument
contraindications: None
references: Beaton DE, Wright JG, Katz JN. Development of the QuickDASH. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2005;87(5):1038-46.

rights.holder: Institute for Work and Health, Toronto

scoring.formula: Externally administered QuickDASH score; when all eleven item scores are summed, score = ((raw sum ÷ 11) - 1) × 25.
